\chapter{Good, Bad, Clever}
\label{ch:mr-good-and-bad}
\hlchaptermodality{51}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can judge a thing good or bad, call a person clever, and deny any of those judgements.}

Complete MR-R51-good-and-bad and make three judgements plus a denial -- the tea is good, the water is bad, my friend is clever, the water is not good.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[chāṅglā]{\mr{चांगला} (chāṅglā) — good}

\label{lesson:MR-C51-changla}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{बरं}} has been in this book since chapter four and it can only say that a STATE is fine — \emph{\mr{मी} \mr{बरा} \mr{आहे}}. It cannot call a thing good.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sundar khoolī}, then name the class \textbf{\mr{सुंदर}} belongs to
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{चांगला}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{चांगला}} — \emph{chāṅglā} — \textbf{good}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{चांगला} \mr{चहा} · \mr{चांगली} \mr{खोली} · \mr{चांगलं} \mr{घर}} — \emph{chāṅglā chahā · chāṅglī khoolī · chāṅglaṁ ghar}
\end{quote}

It ends in \textbf{-\mr{आ}}, so it agrees, and you already know all three forms without being told them. That is the second time the rule has paid for itself.

Keep it apart from \textbf{\mr{बरं}}. \textbf{\mr{बरं}} answers \emph{how are you} and closes a turn — \emph{fine, all right, okay}. \textbf{\mr{चांगला}} is a judgement about a thing: this tea is good, that room is good, he is a good friend. English blurs the two under \emph{good} and Marathi does not.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chāṅglā chahā} — good tea
  \item \emph{chāṅglī khoolī}, \emph{chāṅglaṁ ghar}
  \item \emph{baraṁ} and \emph{chāṅglā} back to back, and name what each is for
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \textbf{\mr{बरं}} and \textbf{\mr{चांगला}} judges a THING? (\textbf{\mr{चांगला}}.) Which class does \textbf{\mr{चांगला}} belong to? (\textbf{The agreeing one — it ends in -\mr{आ}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%9A\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%82\%E0\%A4\%97\%E0\%A4\%B2\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{चांगला}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kharāb]{\mr{खराब} (kharāb) — bad, spoiled}

\label{lesson:MR-C51-kharaab}



\begin{quote}
Half a judgement is not a judgement. You can say a thing is good and not that it is not.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{खराब}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{खराब}} — \emph{kharāb} — \textbf{bad, spoiled, ruined}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{खराब} \mr{पाणी}} — \emph{kharāb pāṇī} — \textbf{bad water}
\end{quote}

Its last letter tells you it will not agree, before you ever hear it used: \textbf{\mr{खराब} \mr{खोली}}, \textbf{\mr{खराब} \mr{घर}}, no ending anywhere. Three adjectives into the class now, and the test has not failed you once.

This one carries its history on its face. It is the Arabic \emph{kharāb}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ruined, in ruins},\textquotedblright{} and it reached Marathi through Persian — the same road that brought \textbf{\mr{मदत}} and \textbf{\mr{हरकत}}, both of which this book has already taught. Centuries of Persian administration in the Deccan left several hundred such words in ordinary Marathi.

The original sense survives in the modern one. \textbf{\mr{खराब}} is closer to \emph{spoiled} than to \emph{evil}: bad water, a bad road, a phone that has stopped working.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kharāb pāṇī} — bad water
  \item \emph{pāṇī kharāb āhe}, then \emph{pāṇī chāṅglaṁ nāhī}
  \item which language it came from, and by which road — \textbf{Arabic, through Persian}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{\mr{खराब}} agree? (\textbf{No — it does not end in -\mr{आ}}.) Which two taught words came by the same road? (\textbf{\mr{मदत}} and \textbf{\mr{हरकत}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%96\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%AC}{Wiktionary: \mr{खराब}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hushār]{\mr{हुशार} (hushār) — clever}

\label{lesson:MR-C51-hushaar}



\begin{quote}
Everything you can describe so far is a thing. The A1 speaking paper asks you to describe a \textbf{person} for a minute.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{हुशार}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{हुशार}} — \emph{hushār} — \textbf{clever, sharp, quick-witted}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{माझा} \mr{मित्र} \mr{हुशार} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{mājhā mitra hushār āhe.} — \textbf{my friend is clever.}
\end{quote}

Another one that does not agree, and by now you saw that coming from the last letter. It is the sixth adjective this book has taught and the fourth that does not agree; the invariable class is already twice the size of the other one, which is worth knowing so the endings stop feeling like the default.

\textbf{\mr{हुशार}} is the Persian \emph{hushyār}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{alert, wide awake},\textquotedblright{} built on \emph{hush}, \textquotedblleft{}consciousness, wits.\textquotedblright{} Marathi kept the alertness inside the cleverness: a \textbf{\mr{हुशार}} person is quick rather than merely learned, and it is what a teacher says about a child who catches on fast.

It is a compliment you can pay out loud without awkwardness, which is not true of every word in this area, and it is exactly the kind of thing the speaking paper's one-minute description wants.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hushār} — clever
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhā mitra hushār āhe}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{puṇyāhūn} and that your clever friend comes from Pune
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Persian \textbf{hush} inside it mean? (\textbf{Wits, consciousness} — so \emph{clever} is \emph{awake}.) Does it agree? (\textbf{No}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B9\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%B6\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%B0}{Wiktionary: \mr{हुशार}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chāṅglā · kharāb · hushār]{Say what you think of something}

\label{lesson:MR-R51-good-and-bad}



\begin{quote}
Three more adjectives. Two of them cannot change and one can. Say which is which before you use any of them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chahā chāṅglā āhe} — and hear the masculine ending
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pāṇī kharāb āhe} — and hear that nothing was added
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhā mitra hushār āhe}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sundar}, \emph{lahān}, \emph{kharāb}, \emph{hushār} — the four that never move
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{udyāpāsūn} and promise something from tomorrow
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Of the six adjectives you now own, how many agree? (\textbf{Two} — \textbf{\mr{मोठा}} and \textbf{\mr{चांगला}}.) What do the other four have in common? (\textbf{None of them ends in -\mr{आ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
